query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, tightly bonded CrTa-rich overlay coating on refractory high-entropy alloys will improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in-situ formation of a continuous, protective CrTaO4-based oxide scale during prolonged oxidation exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) in its as-cast/uncoated state that exhibits relatively high oxidation rates in air at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin CrTa-rich overlay coating (for example, via pack cementation or a comparable surface-engineering technique) to the alloy surface without altering its bulk composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in dry air at temperatures between 1200 °C and 1300 °C for 100 or more hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The CrTa-rich surface layer oxidizes to form a dense and continuous CrTaO4-based oxide scale that mechanically adheres to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The overlay acts as a diffusion barrier by rapidly forming a protective oxide that reduces oxygen ingress into the underlying alloy. This is achieved by facilitating the formation of a CrTaO4-based scale, which has been shown in prior studies to hinder both outward diffusion of metal ions and inward diffusion of oxygen atoms, thereby lowering the overall oxidation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated RHEAs, the coated alloy will exhibit a significantly lower mass gain and maintain a more intact, adherent oxide layer after 100+ hours at 1200–1300 °C, indicating improved oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy, which under identical conditions shows a higher rate of oxygen uptake, less protective (or even non-continuous) oxide scale formation, and potential scale spallation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis pertains to refractory high-entropy alloys suitable for forming stable CrTaO4 scales under high-temperature (1200–1300 °C) air exposure. It may not hold for alloys that do not provide the necessary elements (e.g., sufficient Cr and Ta availability at the surface) or under different environmental conditions (e.g., cyclic thermal loading or humid atmospheres).
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance and long-term adhesion of the overlay under complex service conditions (e.g., thermal cycling) remain to be determined. There is also uncertainty regarding the interplay with secondary oxide phases (e.g., minor Al2O3 or Cr2O3) that could form.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set with the CrTa-rich overlay coating and one uncoated control. Expose both sets to dry air at 1250 °C for 100+ hours in a thermogravimetric furnace. After exposure, analyze the samples for overall mass gain, oxide scale thickness, continuity, and adhesion using SEM, XRD, and image analysis.
measurements: Mass gain (mg/cm2) over the exposure period
Oxide scale morphology and thickness (via SEM cross-sectional analysis)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (using XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass gain or if the CrTaO4-based oxide scale is not continuous and protective (e.g., if scale spallation or comparable damage to the uncoated samples is observed), the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To explore the types of oxides, XRD analysis was performed on the surface of the coatings after oxidation. As shown in Figure 9, the oxide mainly consists of CrTaO4, TiO2, and Cr2O3; the Cr1 alloy has the highest oxide diffraction peak, indicating that more oxides are generated, making the oxide film on the coating surface uniform and dense. The dense oxide film inhibits the diffusion of oxygen atoms, reduces the oxidation rate, and improves oxidation resistance. This conclusion is also consistent with the results presented by the oxide weight-gain curve. The results show that adding Cr to the WVTaTi alloy can effectively improve high-temperature oxidation resistance.

AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. decision.trend: Starting around 2019, researchers focused on creating stable oxide scales to protect refractory HEAs at high temperatures, with one approach involving CrTaO4-based surface oxides (PMC6513993). Follow-up studies examined the role of alloying elements (e.g., Co, Cr) in forming more protective scales (PMC8468823, PMC10142552). Most recently, a high-entropy alloy-based coating was shown to reduce high-temperature oxidation by producing a densely bonded protective layer (PMC10488483). Despite these advances, there is still a demand for a robust surface engineering route that avoids further bulk compositional additions yet ensures a well-bonded, stable oxide scale under severe thermal and oxidizing conditions.
decision.unsolved: While compositional tweaks (adding Cr, Al, or Hf) have improved oxidation resistance, there is no consistent, non-alloying method for reliably controlling oxide-scale formation on refractory HEAs. Achieving a durable, stable, and adherent oxide or barrier layer without altering the bulk composition remains challenging, especially for prolonged, high-temperature service in oxidizing environments.
decision.lever: Deposit (e.g., via pack cementation or similar technique) a thin, tightly bonded CrTa- or CrAl-rich overlay coating that forms a continuous oxide scale at 1200–1300 °C in air for 100+ hours exposure.
decision.why: Prior work (e.g., PMC6513993, PMC10488483) shows that protective surface layers forming robust oxide scales (such as CrTaO4 or Al2O3) can dramatically slow oxygen ingress without changing the alloy composition. A thin, diffusion-barrier coating that stablely forms such an oxide will shield the bulk from excessive oxidation. To validate, a long-duration oxidation test (up to 100 hours in dry air at 1200–1300 °C) could measure mass gain and scale integrity. A falsifying outcome would be rapid scale spallation or oxidation rates comparable to the uncoated alloy.
